items.prompt: Which HTTP method is normally used to retrieve a resource without changing it?

options.label: PUT
DELETE
GET
POST

rubric: GET is the read-only retrieval method.
POST, PUT and DELETE all change server state.

items.prompt: Which status code means a new resource was successfully created?
rubric: 201 Created signals a new resource was made.
200 is generic success, 204 means no content, and 302 is a redirect.

items.prompt: Which URL best follows REST naming conventions for the collection of all orders?

options.label: /getOrders
/createOrders
/orders
/order/list

rubric: REST URLs name resources with plural nouns, and the HTTP method gives the action.
The other options put verbs or actions in the path.

items.prompt: Which status code means the requested resource could not be found?
rubric: 404 Not Found is the code for a missing resource.
400 is a malformed request, 401 is unauthenticated, and 500 is a server error.

items.prompt: What does it mean for an HTTP method to be idempotent?

options.label: Repeating the same request leaves the server in the same state as sending it once
The request can be repeated safely because it only reads data and never changes any server state
The server returns the same status code and identical response body for every repeat of the request
The response can be stored by caches and reused for later requests without contacting the server

rubric: Idempotent means repeated identical requests leave the server in the same state as one request.
Distractors confuse idempotency with security, speed or caching.

items.prompt: Which of these HTTP methods are defined as safe, meaning they should not modify server state? Select all that apply.

options.label: POST
DELETE
OPTIONS
GET
HEAD

rubric: GET, HEAD and OPTIONS are read-only and therefore safe.
POST and DELETE change state, so they are not safe.

items.prompt: A developer is writing a client for a bookstore API. Books live at `/books`, and each has an id. The developer wants to remove the book with id 7. Which request should the client send?

options.label: PUT /books/7
POST /books/7/delete
DELETE /books/7
GET /books/delete?id=7

rubric: DELETE on the resource URL removes that resource.
Distractors put the action in the path or use methods that do not delete.

items.prompt: Why do REST APIs use nouns in URLs, such as `/users`, instead of verbs, such as `/getUsers`?

options.label: The URL names the resource and the HTTP method already says the action
Nouns let the API skip status codes because the URL implies the result
Nouns make the URL shorter, and length decides how fast requests run
Verbs in URLs are rejected by HTTP servers as invalid

rubric: The URL identifies the resource while the method expresses the action, which keeps APIs consistent.
Distractors invent technical limits or performance effects that do not exist.

items.prompt: How do PUT and PATCH differ when updating a resource?

options.label: PUT only creates resources, while PATCH only deletes fields from them
They are identical and differ only in which browsers support them
PATCH replaces the whole resource, while PUT changes only the fields sent
PUT replaces the whole resource, while PATCH changes only the fields sent

rubric: PUT sends a full replacement; PATCH sends a partial update.
The strongest distractor swaps the two meanings.

items.prompt: A client sends the same `POST /orders` request with an identical body twice. What will typically happen in a standard REST API?

options.label: One order is created, because the server detects the duplicate body
Two separate orders are created, because POST is not idempotent
The second request is rejected, because POST can only run once
The first order is overwritten, because POST replaces existing data

rubric: POST is not idempotent, so each call usually creates a new resource.
Distractors treat POST like PUT or assume automatic duplicate detection.

items.prompt: A user is logged in with a valid token but tries to delete another person's account and is not allowed to. Which status code fits best?

options.label: 401 Unauthorized
409 Conflict
403 Forbidden
404 Not Found

rubric: 403 means the identity is known but lacks permission.
401 is for missing or invalid authentication, which is the usual confusion.

items.prompt: Why should an API paginate a collection such as `/products` with thousands of items?

options.label: Pagination lets the server skip authentication checks on every page after the first request
Pagination encrypts the data in transit so that only the page being viewed can be read
Returning everything at once is slow and heavy, so clients fetch it in pages
HTTP itself requires pagination and caps every single response at 100 items per request

rubric: Pages keep responses small and fast and reduce load on server and client.
Distractors invent security or protocol rules that do not exist.

items.prompt: Which of these are good reasons to version a public REST API, for example with `/v1/` and `/v2/`? Select all that apply.

options.label: Breaking changes can ship without breaking existing clients
Every small bug fix should get its own new version number
Clients can migrate to the new version on their own schedule
Versioning removes the need to document the API

rubric: Versions let breaking changes coexist with old clients and give them time to migrate.
Versioning does not replace documentation, and minor bug fixes do not need new versions.

items.prompt: A team's API returns HTTP 200 with the body `{"error": "user not found"}` when a requested user does not exist. A client developer complains that this is hard to work with. What is the main problem with this design?

options.label: The 200 status says success, so clients and caches can't tell it failed
The error message is too brief, so it should list every field that was searched
The error body should be XML, since JSON is not suited to carrying error details
The response should use 500, since a missing user means the server failed to respond

rubric: Status codes should reflect the outcome, so a missing resource should return 404.
Distractors misplace the issue on body format, server-error codes or message length.

items.prompt: Why do REST APIs favour URLs like `/orders` over `/getOrders`?

options.label: Clients cache only URLs that contain nouns, so verbs would disable all caching
The HTTP method already states the action, so the URL only needs to name the resource
Nouns in URLs make responses smaller, so the API runs faster over slow networks
Verbs in URLs are rejected by most web servers, so action words must be avoided

rubric: The method (GET, POST, ...) carries the action, so the URL identifies the resource.
Distractors invent technical limits on verbs in URLs; it is a convention, not a server restriction.

items.prompt: A method is described as idempotent. What does that mean for `PUT /users/5` sent three times with the same body?

options.label: Each call creates a new user, and the server assigns three different ids
The server state after three calls is the same as after one call
Only the first call is processed and later ones are rejected with an error
The response body must be identical every time, including any timestamps

rubric: Idempotent means repeating the request has the same effect on server state as sending it once.
Distractors confuse idempotency with rejecting duplicates or with identical response bodies.

items.prompt: A client calls `GET /users/999`, well-formed and authorised, but no user 999 exists. Which status code should the API return?

options.label: 403 Forbidden, because the client is not allowed to see user 999
200 OK, with an empty body to show nothing was found
500 Internal Server Error, because the lookup did not succeed
404 Not Found, because the requested resource does not exist

rubric: 404 signals that the identified resource does not exist.
Distractors mistake a missing resource for a server fault, a success, or a permission problem.

items.prompt: What is the main purpose of pagination on `GET /products` when the catalogue has 200,000 items?

options.label: It sorts the products so the newest ones always appear first
It compresses large result sets so they download much faster
It stops clients from requesting the same product twice
It returns the collection in small, manageable chunks

rubric: Pagination limits response size and load by splitting large collections into pages.
Distractors attribute security, sorting or deduplication to pagination, which it does not provide.

items.prompt: Which of these HTTP methods is classified as safe, meaning it should not change server state?

options.label: GET
POST
PUT
DELETE

rubric: GET is a safe read-only method.
PUT and DELETE are idempotent but change state; POST is neither safe nor idempotent.

items.prompt: Why is it good practice for an API to return every error in one consistent JSON format? Select all that apply.

options.label: Clients can write one error-handling routine for all endpoints
Developers can read the cause and fix their requests more easily
It guarantees that no errors will occur in the API
It removes the need to use HTTP status codes at all

rubric: A consistent format simplifies client code and makes errors easier to understand.
Error bodies complement status codes rather than replace them, and they cannot prevent errors.

items.prompt: A team runs `/v1/customers`, where `name` is one string. They want to split it into `first_name` and `last_name`, which would break existing mobile apps that read `name`. They plan to publish `/v2/customers` and keep `/v1` running for a while. What is the main reason for this approach?

options.label: It makes the old and new formats share one codebase, so the team maintains fewer endpoints
It lets the URL signal which fields exist, so clients can skip reading the documentation
It ships the breaking change while existing clients keep working until they migrate
It gives clients a cached copy of the new format, so the v2 responses load faster for them

rubric: Versioning lets breaking changes ship without breaking existing consumers.
Distractors claim speed, no documentation needed, or forced upgrades, which versioning does not do.

items.prompt: You need an endpoint returning all comments on the post with id 7. Which request follows REST naming conventions?

options.label: `GET /posts/7/comments`
`POST /posts/7/comments/list`
`GET /getComments?post=7`
`GET /comments/post/fetch/7`

rubric: Nested plural nouns express that comments belong to post 7, and GET reads.
Distractors put verbs in the path or use POST for a read.

items.prompt: `POST /invoices` successfully creates invoice 310. Which response best fits REST conventions?

options.label: `200 OK` with the text "done" and no other information
`201 Created` with a `Location: /invoices/310` header
`202 Accepted` with a `Location: /invoices` header
`204 No Content` with no header pointing to the new invoice

rubric: 201 plus a Location header tells the client where the new resource lives.
Distractors give a generic success, hide the new URL, or imply asynchronous processing.

items.prompt: A user record has 12 fields. A client wants to change only the email of user 12. Which request is the best fit?

options.label: `POST /users/12/changeEmail` with the full 12-field record in the body
`PATCH /users/12` with body `{"email": "new@example.com"}`
`PUT /users/12` with only `{"email": "new@example.com"}` in the body
`GET /users/12?email=new@example.com` to update the email

rubric: PATCH applies a partial update to the resource.
PUT expects a full replacement, so a one-field PUT could wipe the other fields; GET must not modify state.

items.prompt: An API uses `offset` and `limit` for pagination. With a page size of 20, which query returns the third page, counting from page 1?

options.label: `?offset=20&limit=40`
`?offset=3&limit=20`
`?offset=40&limit=20`
`?offset=60&limit=20`

rubric: Page 3 skips 2 pages x 20 = 40 items, so offset=40.
Distractors skip three pages, change the limit, or treat offset as a page number.

items.prompt: `DELETE /sessions/abc` successfully removes the session. The API has nothing useful to return in the body. Which status code should it send?

options.label: `301 Moved Permanently`
`201 Created`
`100 Continue`
`204 No Content`

rubric: 204 means success with no response body, which fits a delete.
Other codes describe creation, redirection or an interim response.

items.prompt: Which of these requests are designed in line with REST conventions? Select all that apply.

options.label: `DELETE /orders/88` to remove order 88
`GET /users/5/orders` to list the orders of user 5
`GET /orders/88/delete` to remove order 88
`POST /users/5/deleteOrder` to remove an order

rubric: Nested resource reads with GET and removals with DELETE on the resource URL are conventional.
The other two put the action in the URL, and a GET that deletes breaks the safe-method rule.

items.prompt: A client sends `POST /users` with syntactically valid JSON, `{"name": "Ana"}`, but the API requires an `email` field too. You are implementing the handler. Which response is best?

options.label: `404 Not Found`, because the required email resource was not found
`500 Internal Server Error`, because the user could not be saved without it
`400 Bad Request` with a JSON error body naming the missing `email`
`200 OK` with `{"status": "failed", "reason": "email is missing"}` in the body

rubric: A client mistake gets a 4xx code, and the body should say which field is wrong.
Distractors hide the failure in a 200, misuse 404, or blame the server with 500.

items.prompt: A client sends `POST /articles` and the server successfully creates the article, which is now available at `/articles/981`. Which response best follows REST conventions?

options.label: 201 Created, with a Location header pointing to /articles/981
200 OK, returning the new article in the response body
202 Accepted, with a Location header pointing to /articles/981
204 No Content, since the client already sent the data

rubric: 201 Created plus a Location header tells the client the resource now exists and where to find it.
202 means processing is not finished, and plain 200 or 204 omit the new resource's location.

items.prompt: You must let clients fetch the comments on post 7 written by author 3. Which endpoint is the best resource-oriented design?

options.label: GET /getComments?post=7&author=3
GET /posts/7/comments/author/3
GET /posts/7/comments?author=3
POST /posts/7/comments/search?author=3

rubric: The collection is nested under its parent and filtering is a query parameter on a GET.
Distractors use a verb in the path, treat a filter as a sub-resource, or use POST for a read.

items.prompt: An API uses `?offset=&limit=` pagination with `limit=25` and offsets start at 0. Which offset returns the 4th page?
rubric: Page 4 skips 3 pages of 25 items, so offset = 75.
100 is the common off-by-one error and 4 confuses page number with offset.

items.prompt: Which change to an existing, widely used API version is backward-compatible for current clients?

options.label: Changing `id` from an integer to a string for flexibility
Renaming the response field `name` to `full_name` for clarity
Making the optional `status` query parameter required for safety
Adding a new optional `nickname` field to existing responses

rubric: Adding an optional response field is additive, and well-behaved clients ignore unknown fields.
Renames, type changes and newly required parameters break existing callers.

items.prompt: A valid token for user A is used to call `GET /orders/42`, which belongs to user B. The API deliberately reveals that the order exists but refuses access. Which status fits?

options.label: 404, because the caller cannot see the order
400, because the request asks for the wrong order
401, because the caller must authenticate again
403, because the caller is known but not permitted

rubric: 403 means the caller is authenticated but lacks permission for this resource.
401 is for missing or invalid credentials, and 404 hides existence, which the prompt rules out.

items.prompt: Which requests are idempotent, so a client may safely retry them automatically after a timeout? Select all that apply.

options.label: `PUT /users/5` with a full replacement body
`PATCH /users/5` with body `{"loginCount": {"increment": 1}}`
`POST /users` creating a new user on each call
`DELETE /users/5`

items.prompt: A profile resource has 20 fields. A mobile app lets users change only their phone number, and the team does not want to resend or overwrite the other 19 fields. Which request should the app send?

options.label: PATCH /profiles/9 sending only the phone field
POST /profiles/9/update-phone sending the phone field
GET /profiles/9 with the new phone as a query parameter
PUT /profiles/9 sending only the phone field

rubric: PATCH is meant for partial updates, so only the changed field is sent.
PUT with a partial body would replace the whole resource and wipe the other fields.

items.prompt: A feed API uses `?offset=&limit=20`, newest first. Users scrolling see some items twice, and new posts arrive every few seconds. What is the root cause?

options.label: New inserts at the top shift older items down, so later offsets re-cover seen items
Sorting newest first is unstable, so the database returns rows in a different random order on every page request
The limit of 20 is too small, so consecutive pages overlap by a few items at their shared boundaries
Offsets are zero-based, so each page repeats the last item of the previous page at its start

rubric: Offset pagination is positional, so inserts before the current position push items into the next page.
Page size, sort direction and zero-based offsets do not cause duplicates by themselves.

items.prompt: An API returns `200 OK` with an error message in the body for missing resources. Dashboards show a 0% error rate while users complain of failures. Why does this design cause the problem?

options.label: Clients cannot parse JSON error messages unless the status is exactly 404
Tools key off status codes, so failures sent as 200 look like successes to them
Servers return 200 faster than 404, so latency metrics become skewed and misleading
HTTP forbids a JSON body from containing an error field when the status is 200

rubric: Monitoring, caches, retries and client libraries rely on status codes to detect failure.
The other options invent rules about bodies, parsing or latency that HTTP does not impose.

items.prompt: Customers are charged twice when the mobile app times out on `POST /payments` and retries. Which fix addresses the root cause?

options.label: Add rate limiting so the client cannot send two payment requests within a few seconds of each other
Switch the endpoint to GET so that a retried request is safe to repeat without side effects
Require an `Idempotency-Key` header and return the stored result for repeats
Raise the client timeout so the response usually arrives before any retry would be sent

rubric: The server cannot tell a retry from a new payment; an idempotency key lets it deduplicate.
Longer timeouts and rate limits do not remove duplicates, and GET must not change state.

items.prompt: After a search crawler indexed an admin page, several users vanished. Their deletion endpoint is `GET /users/5/delete`. What is the underlying design flaw?

options.label: A state change is exposed through GET, which crawlers may call freely
The endpoint should return 200 rather than 204 so crawlers know the deletion succeeded
The verb `delete` is placed in the path, which breaks the API's resource naming style
User ids should be passed in the query string instead of the URL path to avoid indexing

rubric: GET is defined as safe, so tools assume it can be called without side effects.
The other options address style or status codes, not why the deletions happened.

items.prompt: A team compares URL versioning (`/v2/orders`) with header versioning (`Accept: application/vnd.shop.v2+json`). Which statement correctly analyses the trade-off?

options.label: URL versions are invisible to shared caches, so they need a `Vary` header to avoid serving wrong versions
Header versioning keeps URIs stable, but is harder to test in a browser and needs `Vary` for caches
Header versioning moves clients to the newest version at once, since the server picks the media type
URL versioning gives one resource several URIs, so clients that send a custom header see a different identity

rubric: Header versioning keeps one URI per resource but hides the version from simple tools and cache keys.
URL versions are visible to caches, and neither scheme forces clients to upgrade automatically.

items.prompt: A team lists these endpoints. Which ones violate consistent REST naming and method conventions? Select all that apply.

options.label: `PUT /users/5/Profile` mixes capitalised and lowercase path segments
`POST /getUsers` puts a verb in the path and uses POST to read data
`GET /users/5/orders` nests orders under their owning user
`DELETE /order?id=3` uses a singular noun and a query parameter to identify the resource

rubric: Verbs in paths, singular names with query-string identity and inconsistent casing break conventions.
Nesting a collection under its owner is a standard, consistent pattern.

items.prompt: A product list is sorted by `price` and paginated with a cursor holding the last `price` seen, so the next page uses `price > cursor`. Clients report that some products never appear, mostly cheap ones. Many products share the same price. What is the cause and fix?

options.label: The page size is too small; raise the limit so ties never straddle a page boundary
Price is a float; store prices as strings so that comparisons stay exact across pages
Cursors expire too quickly; extend the cursor lifetime so clients can finish paging
Ties at a page boundary are skipped by `>`; sort by price then id and cursor on both

rubric: A non-unique sort key with a strict comparison drops tied items; a unique tiebreaker makes the cursor unambiguous.
Expiry, float type and page size do not explain the missing items or reliably remove ties.

items.prompt: A client retries `POST /payments` after a network timeout and customers are occasionally charged twice. The server processes each request it receives independently. Which root cause best explains the duplicate charges?

options.label: POST is not idempotent and the API gives the server no way to recognise a retried request as the same operation
POST responses cannot be cached, so the client resends the request until it receives a fresh response
The endpoint should have returned 202 Accepted, because 201 Created tells clients to retry the call
The URL uses a plural noun, which makes the server treat each request as a new collection entry

rubric: Without an idempotency key or similar, a retried POST is indistinguishable from a new one, so it is processed twice.
Distractors confuse caching, status codes and URL naming with retry safety.

items.prompt: An API's `GET /orders?page=3&per_page=50` sometimes shows the same order on two consecutive pages while new orders are being created at the top of the list. What is the most likely cause?

options.label: Offset pagination shifts when rows are inserted ahead of the offset, so items move between pages
The sort column is not unique, so rows with equal values come back in a random order on each request
The per_page value of 50 is above the maximum page size HTTP permits, so the server repeats rows
A shared proxy caches each query string separately, so adjacent pages are served from overlapping snapshots

rubric: Inserts at the head push existing rows to later offsets, producing duplicates or skips.
Distractors invent HTTP limits or blame stable sorting and caching.

items.prompt: A team's `PUT /users/42` handler replaces the user with the request body. A mobile client sends only `{"email": "a@b.com"}` and users report their names disappearing. What does the analysis show?

options.label: The email field must be moved into the URL path, because PUT treats every field left in the body as optional and unchanged
PUT is only valid for creating new resources, so the server wiped the existing record before recreating it from the body
PUT has full-replacement semantics, so omitted fields are dropped; partial updates belong under PATCH
The server should return 204 instead of 200, because a 200 response makes clients clear any fields they did not send

rubric: PUT replaces the whole representation; partial changes should use PATCH.
Distractors misattribute the loss to status codes or claim PUT only creates.

items.prompt: An API returns 200 with `{"error": "not found"}` for missing resources. Monitoring shows a 0% error rate while customers complain. Which consequence of this design best explains the gap?

options.label: Status 200 is only sent for POST requests, so GET failures are logged under a separate metric
HTTP forbids a JSON body on a 200 response, so monitoring discards those requests entirely
Tools, caches and clients keyed on status codes see every response as a success, hiding failures
The error text is too short for monitoring to classify, which makes it count as a redirect

rubric: Intermediaries and monitors rely on the status line, so errors hidden in 200 bodies go unseen.
Distractors state false HTTP rules.

items.prompt: A v1 API's `GET /products/7` returned `price` as a string like "9.99". A developer changes it to a number in place, and several partner integrations break, though no endpoint was removed. Which analysis is correct?

options.label: Numbers and strings are interchangeable in JSON, so the breakage came from the payload growing larger and hitting partners' response size limits
Changing a field's type breaks consumers that parse it, even though the URL and field name stay the same
Only removed endpoints or renamed fields can break clients, so the partners must have been relying on undocumented URLs or behaviour
The change was safe, but partners had cached the old 200 responses and replayed them against the new schema, causing parse errors

rubric: Type changes break strictly typed or parsing consumers; compatibility covers schema, not only URLs.
Distractors dismiss schema changes as non-breaking.

items.prompt: A `GET /reports?from=2024-01-01` endpoint is slow and its responses are never served from a shared cache, though the data changes hourly. Which findings could explain the missing cache hits? Select all that apply.

options.label: The response sends `Cache-Control: no-store`
The endpoint is a GET, which makes it uncacheable by definition
The response carries `Vary: *`, preventing reuse across requests
The response lacks validators such as `ETag` or `Last-Modified` and any freshness lifetime

rubric: no-store, absent freshness/validators and Vary: * each block shared cache reuse.
GET is the canonical cacheable method, so that option is false.

items.prompt: A team exposes `POST /orders/{id}/cancel`. A new engineer finds that cancelling an already-shipped order returns 200 with an unchanged order, and the support team cannot tell whether cancellations worked. Which diagnosis fits best?

options.label: The endpoint hides a state conflict; it should reject the invalid transition with 409 and a machine-readable reason
The 200 status is correct for a no-op, but the response should drop its body so that support can see the failure clearly
Cancelling should return 404 once an order has shipped, because the cancel action no longer exists for that order at all
The verb in the path breaks REST naming rules, so the cancel should be a PUT or DELETE and then the 200 would be accurate

rubric: Invalid state transitions are conflicts; 409 with a reason makes outcomes observable.
Distractors misdiagnose via naming purity, body removal or 404 misuse.

items.prompt: You must paginate a feed of 50 million events that receives constant inserts. Criteria: stable results while paging, consistent performance deep into the list, and clients only moving forward. Which design best meets them?

options.label: Cursor (keyset) pagination using an opaque token encoding the last seen sort key and id
Offset pagination with a larger default page size so fewer deep pages are requested
Offset pagination with `page` and `per_page`, since it is the simplest for clients to compute
Returning the whole feed in one response and letting clients slice it locally

rubric: Keyset cursors stay stable under inserts and avoid deep-offset scans.
Offset variants shift under inserts and slow with depth.

items.prompt: A public API has many third-party clients you cannot force to upgrade. Criteria: existing clients must never break, new capabilities must ship regularly, and maintenance cost should stay low. Which versioning approach is the best trade-off?

options.label: Change fields in place and announce changes by email a few weeks ahead, since consumers should keep up with the API
Add fields without breaking existing ones, and release a new major version only rarely, with a long deprecation window
Release a new major version for every field addition and keep all old versions running, so each client pins an exact schema
Drop explicit versions and let each client negotiate fields through query flags that are documented only in release notes

rubric: Additive evolution plus rare, well-announced major versions balances stability and cost.
Distractors either explode maintenance or break clients.

items.prompt: Choose the best error response for a failed validation on `POST /users`, given criteria: clients must programmatically identify which fields failed, humans must read the cause, and the format should follow a widely adopted standard.

options.label: Return 400 with an empty body, since the status code alone tells clients the request was invalid and which input to fix
Return 422 or 400 with an `application/problem+json` body (RFC 9457) with type, title, detail and per-field errors
Return 200 with `{"ok": false, "error": "invalid"}` so every client can parse a single response shape for all outcomes
Return 400 with a plain text message such as "name is required", written clearly so that any developer can read the cause

rubric: A standard problem-details body with field errors serves machines and humans.
Distractors misuse status codes or omit structure.

items.prompt: Two URL designs for line items of an order are proposed. A: `/orders/{id}/items/{itemId}`. B: `/items/{itemId}`, with `orderId` as a query filter. Items never exist outside an order and are always accessed with their order. Which judgement is best?

options.label: B, because a flat URL lets you check access on the item alone without loading the order first
B, because flat URLs keep paths short and make caching easier for every kind of child resource
A, because the HTTP specification requires child resources to be nested under their parent path
A, because the path shows ownership so access checks and lifecycle follow the order

rubric: Nesting fits strict containment and eases scoping and access checks.
Distractors claim false universals or spec requirements.

items.prompt: A long-running video export takes up to 10 minutes. Criteria: HTTP connections should not be held open, clients need progress, and results must be retrievable afterwards. Which design is best?

options.label: Hold the POST open until finished and raise server timeouts to 15 minutes
Return 201 immediately with an empty file URL that returns 200 and a partial file until ready
Return 200 with the final file URL before the work starts, and tell clients to retry on failures
Return 202 Accepted with a `Location` to a job resource that clients poll for status and result link

rubric: The async job pattern with 202 and a status resource meets all criteria.
Distractors hold connections, expose partial results or misreport status.

items.prompt: You are reviewing a design for `GET /search` that accepts a complex filter, sometimes 20 KB long. Criteria: keep semantics honest, stay cacheable where practical, and avoid URL length failures. Which judgements are sound? Select all that apply.

options.label: Saving a complex filter as a resource and fetching results by its id can restore cacheability
Every search must use POST, since GET can never carry filters
Short, common filters should stay on GET with query parameters so they remain cacheable
A POST-based search endpoint is a defensible trade-off for oversized filters, documented as safe-in-effect

rubric: Hybrid designs balance cacheability and URL limits.
GET carries filters fine; 'always POST' is overreach.

items.prompt: Your team must rate-limit a public API. Criteria: clients should self-throttle without guessing, bursts from one client must not starve others, and responses must be standard. A teammate proposes silently dropping requests over the limit. Which alternative is best?

options.label: Return 503 for every limited request so clients assume the whole service is down
Close the TCP connection without a response, because limited clients should reconnect later
Return 200 with an empty body so clients do not trigger error handling
Return 429 with a `Retry-After` header and documented rate-limit headers, enforced per client key

rubric: 429 with Retry-After lets clients back off per key predictably.
Distractors mislead clients or give no signal.

items.prompt: A feed API holds 20M rows and receives constant inserts at the head. Criteria: no duplicated or skipped items while a client pages, and roughly constant cost for deep pages. Which pagination design best meets both?

options.label: Offset and limit with a larger default page size to reduce the number of pages
Keyset cursor on (created_at, id), returning an opaque next cursor with each page
Offset and limit, because page numbers are simple for clients and stay stable even while new rows are inserted at the head
Page numbers plus a cached total count that is refreshed once every minute

rubric: Keyset pagination anchors on the last seen sort key, so inserts do not shift pages and deep pages use an index seek.
Offset-based options shift under inserts and get slower with depth; learners assume page numbers are stable.

items.prompt: Clients retry POST /payments after network timeouts and sometimes double-charge. Criteria: safe retries, no guessing of client intent, minimal client burden. Which fix is best?

options.label: Require a client-generated Idempotency-Key; store it with the first result and replay that result on repeats
Reject any POST from the same customer within five minutes as a duplicate, returning 409
Deduplicate by matching customer and amount, because identical requests in a short window almost certainly mean the same charge
Document that clients must never retry a POST and should call GET to check the outcome

rubric: A client-supplied key lets the server distinguish a retry from a new intent and return the stored result.
Heuristic dedupe wrongly blocks legitimate repeat purchases; forbidding retries pushes the burden onto clients.

items.prompt: A teammate wants to ship /v2 because a response gains a new optional field `currency`. Third-party clients upgrade slowly. Judge the proposal against two criteria: avoid breaking clients and avoid version sprawl.

options.label: Sound: the published API description is a contract, so a new field must be released as a new version before clients can rely on it
Unnecessary only if the field is added to all other endpoints too, since mixed response shapes in one version would confuse clients
Unnecessary: an optional field is backward compatible for tolerant clients, so add it to v1 and document it
Sound: clients that validate responses strictly could fail on any new field, so every such change needs its own major version

rubric: Additive, optional changes are non-breaking under the tolerant reader principle, so a major version is wasteful.
Distractors treat any change as breaking or tie compatibility to unrelated uniformity or documentation.

items.prompt: In a multi-tenant API, a user from tenant A requests GET /invoices/9001, which exists but belongs to tenant B. Criteria: do not leak the existence of other tenants' data, and stay consistent with truly missing IDs. Which response is best?

options.label: 401 Unauthorized, because the credentials are not valid for that tenant's data
404 Not Found, identical to the response for an ID that does not exist
403 Forbidden, because the caller is authenticated but lacks permission, and an honest status helps client debugging
200 with an empty body, so the client never sees an error status

rubric: Returning the same 404 for foreign and missing IDs prevents enumeration of other tenants' resources.
403 reveals that the resource exists; 401 is about authentication, not authorisation.

items.prompt: A profile resource has a nullable `middle_name`, where a stored null is meaningful and distinct from 'unchanged'. Clients must also edit single elements of an `emails` array. Which PATCH format best fits these criteria?

options.label: PUT with the full document, because replacing everything avoids ambiguity and removes any need for partial array edits
JSON Patch (RFC 6902) with explicit operations, since it can set null distinctly and address array elements
A custom POST /update-profile endpoint, because standard PATCH formats cannot express null in a way servers can read
JSON Merge Patch, because omitted fields stay unchanged and null cleanly stores a null value

rubric: Merge Patch treats null as 'delete', so it cannot store null and replaces arrays wholesale; JSON Patch uses explicit ops and paths.
Full PUT fails the partial array edit need and risks lost updates.

items.prompt: A service cancels an order when a client calls `GET /orders/17/cancel` and returns 200. Which criticisms of this design are valid? Select all that apply.

options.label: A state-changing GET may only return 3xx codes, so 200 is invalid for this request
A verb in any URI automatically breaks REST, so the endpoint would be invalid whatever method it used
GET is defined as safe, so prefetchers, crawlers or link checkers can cancel orders unintentionally
Intermediaries may cache or replay GET responses, so a cancellation might be skipped or repeated

rubric: The core problem is GET semantics: safety and cacheability are violated.
Verbs in URIs are a style concern, and there is no rule restricting GET status codes in that way.

items.prompt: One tenant's batch job sends 500 requests per second and slows the API. The gateway currently returns 503 to everyone when CPU is high, so other tenants fail too. Criteria: protect other tenants, let well-behaved clients recover automatically, and make the cause visible. Which change is best?

options.label: Return 400 to the heavy tenant, because its request pattern is malformed and should be rejected as invalid
Per-tenant rate limits that return 429 with a Retry-After header to the offending tenant
Keep 503 for all callers but add a Retry-After header so that every client waits the same amount of time
Return 500 with an explanatory message so clients treat the overload as a server bug and raise an alert

rubric: 429 with Retry-After isolates the heavy tenant, tells it what to do and leaves others unaffected.
Shared 503s still hurt everyone; 400 and 500 misdescribe the problem.

items.prompt: Generating a report takes up to 10 minutes. Design constraints: no connection held open, clients can discover progress, and the finished file is fetchable by URL. Which design meets all three?

options.label: POST /reports returns 201 with the file URL immediately; GET on that URL returns 404 until the file is ready
GET /reports?generate=true returns 200 and streams progress lines until the file has finished
POST /reports returns 202 with a Location to a status resource; when finished, the status links to the file
POST /reports holds the connection open and returns 200 with the file, after raising every timeout to fifteen minutes

rubric: 202 plus a pollable status resource frees the connection, exposes progress and links to the result.
Other options hold connections, offer no progress signal or misuse GET.

items.prompt: Two editors may PUT the same document. Design constraints: no lost updates, no server locks held between requests, and clients that omit a precondition must be detected. Which design meets all?

options.label: Lock the document when it is read and release the lock when the same client sends its PUT or after a timeout expires
Return an ETag on GET; require If-Match on PUT; answer 412 on mismatch and 428 if the header is missing
Accept every PUT and keep the one with the latest client timestamp, discarding the older update entirely
Return an ETag on GET; honour If-None-Match on PUT so that only unseen versions are accepted

rubric: If-Match with 412 and 428 gives optimistic concurrency without locks and flags missing preconditions.
Locks violate the constraint, last-write-wins loses updates, and If-None-Match is the wrong precondition.

items.prompt: Design the error body for a public API. Constraints: a stable machine-readable category independent of language, a human-readable detail, field-level validation errors, and room for extension. Which design meets all?

options.label: A JSON body with a numeric internal error code and a localised message string, with field errors packed into the message text
application/problem+json with a type URI, title, status, detail and an `errors` array of field and message pairs
A JSON body with an `error` string holding the English exception class name, plus a `fields` map of field names to messages
Return 200 with `{"success": false, "message": "..."}` and localise the message per Accept-Language for clients to parse

rubric: Problem Details gives a stable type URI, human detail and allows extension members for field errors.
Localised messages as the only signal, bare status codes and stack traces are not stable or safe machine contracts.

items.prompt: Users belong to many groups. Design constraints: add or remove a single membership, adding the same membership twice must be harmless, and clients can list a group's members and a user's groups. Which design meets all?

options.label: PATCH /users/{u} with a full replacement `groups` array, listing a group's members by scanning every user record
PUT and DELETE on /groups/{g}/members/{u}, plus GET /groups/{g}/members and GET /users/{u}/groups
POST /groups/{g}/members with a user id to add, GET to list members, and POST /groups/{g}/remove-member to take a member out
POST /memberships to add, which creates a new record on every call, with listing only through query-string filters

rubric: PUT and DELETE on the membership URI are idempotent and the two GETs cover both directions.
POST-based adds create duplicates, and array replacement is coarse and cannot list members efficiently.

items.prompt: You must retire a v1 endpoint. Constraints: clients get a machine-readable warning, a stated end date, and you can identify who still calls it. Which plan meets all three?

options.label: Redirect v1 calls to v2 with a 301, log which clients follow it, and tell clients to update their saved URLs when convenient
Send Deprecation and Sunset headers linking to migration docs, log calls per API key, and contact remaining callers
Keep v1 running with no end date, remove it from the docs, and watch per-key traffic until usage falls to a low level
Announce the retirement on the blog and list the date there, then return 410 Gone to v1 callers when the sunset date arrives

rubric: Deprecation and Sunset headers give machine-readable notice and date, while per-key logs identify stragglers.
Other options give no header warning, break clients abruptly or lack an end date.

items.prompt: You are designing the pagination cursor for a feed sorted by created_at. Which elements make the design robust? Select all that apply.

options.label: Bind the token to the sort order and filters, rejecting reuse with different parameters using 400
Make the token opaque (such as base64 or signed) so server internals can change without breaking clients
Embed the page number and offset so the server can compute the next page with a SQL OFFSET
Document that clients may build their own cursors from timestamps for convenience
Encode the last item's created_at plus a unique id tiebreaker, so equal timestamps neither repeat nor skip items

rubric: A unique tiebreaker, an opaque token and parameter binding keep keyset paging correct and evolvable.
Offsets reintroduce drift, and client-built cursors turn internals into a public contract.

items.prompt: Mobile apps in the wild read `name` from GET /users/{id}. The team must rename it to `full_name` for consistency. Constraints: existing apps keep working without updates, new clients can use the new name, and removal of the old field must be driven by data. Which plan meets all?

options.label: Return `full_name` only when clients send an opt-in header, leave `name` in place for everyone else, and never remove it, so no client is ever broken
Rename it in place in v1, since JSON clients ignore missing fields and fall back to defaults
Return both `name` and `full_name`, mark `name` deprecated, track its use per client, and remove it once usage reaches zero
Rename it in place and release /v2 only, telling app owners to update before the old field disappears from v1 on a fixed date

rubric: Serving both fields keeps old apps working, and usage tracking makes removal data-driven.
Renaming in place breaks apps that read `name`; keeping both forever fails the data-driven removal constraint.
